correlates.name: Vasopressin Resistance (AVP-R / Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus), including Lithium-Induced
correlates.presentation: Polyuria and polydipsia despite adequate or high ADH.
correlates.pathophysiology: The collecting duct cannot respond to ADH (vasopressin), so free water is lost and the patient has polyuria. Lithium is a major acquired cause.
correlates.treatment: Discontinue lithium if possible, then thiazide diuretic + low-sodium, low-protein diet (low solute load) + an NSAID.

correlates.name: Calcium Nephrolithiasis from Idiopathic Hypercalciuria
correlates.pathophysiology: Excess urinary calcium supersaturates the urine with calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate, seeding recurrent stones.
correlates.treatment: A thiazide reduces urinary calcium by the DCT mechanism above, lowering supersaturation and reducing recurrence in selected patients. Never the only measure - combine with increased fluid intake, dietary modification, weight loss and drug therapy.

correlates.name: Thiazide-Induced Hyponatremia
correlates.pathophysiology: NCC inhibition leaves solute in the tubular fluid, so solute-free water cannot be excreted. Concentrating ability is preserved - the medullary gradient is untouched, the collecting duct still answers ADH, AQP2 is inserted, and free water is reabsorbed.

correlates.name: Liddle Syndrome (Pseudoaldosteronism)
correlates.presentation: Hypertension with hypokalemia in a young patient.
correlates.pathophysiology: Rare autosomal dominant gain-of-function mutation in the genes regulating ENaC, producing far more channels than normal. Unregulated sodium reabsorption creates a strong lumen-negative potential, driving potassium and hydrogen secretion.
correlates.treatment: ENaC inhibitor plus sodium restriction, which manages both the hypertension and the hypokalemia.

correlates.name: Ascites due to Hepatic Cirrhosis
correlates.pathophysiology: Portal hypertension raises hydrostatic pressure and transudes fluid into the peritoneum, lowering effective circulating volume.
correlates.treatment: Spironolactone is first-line, because the patient is in a state of secondary hyperaldosteronism and the drug attacks that directly. It may be given with furosemide, but furosemide is not used alone here.

correlates.name: Triple Hit: Thiazide plus MRA plus NSAID
correlates.presentation: A 70-year-old woman on hydrochlorothiazide and spironolactone starts daily OTC naproxen for knee pain; labs show rising creatinine and potassium 5.8 mEq/L (Slide 37).
correlates.pathophysiology: (1) The thiazide reduces effective circulating volume and renal perfusion pressure, so GFR becomes prostaglandin-dependent on afferent dilation.

correlates.name: Mannitol-Induced Pulmonary Edema
correlates.presentation: A 65-year-old man treated with IV mannitol for traumatic brain injury improves neurologically, then hours later develops dyspnea, crackles, falling oxygen saturation and bilateral pulmonary edema on imaging (Slide 46).
correlates.pathophysiology: Mannitol stays extracellular and raises plasma osmolality; water is pulled from the intracellular to the interstitial to the intravascular compartment, rapidly expanding plasma volume.

drugs.name: Hydrochlorothiazide
drugs.mechanism: Blocks the Na+-Cl- cotransporter (NCC) in the distal convoluted tubule, preventing reabsorption of 5-10% of the filtered sodium load
drugs.indication: First-line for hypertension — an acute fall in ECF and cardiac output gives way to a sustained drop in peripheral vascular resistance
drugs.adverseEffects: Hyponatremia (the classic diuretic cause), hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, hyperuricemia, hyperglycemia and hypercalcemia, over a 6-12 hour duration

drugs.name: Chlorthalidone
drugs.mechanism: Thiazide-like NCC blockade without a benzothiadiazine ring, with a 40-60 hour half-life giving 24-72 hours of action
drugs.indication: Hypertension when smoother 24-hour blood pressure control is wanted; cardiovascular outcomes equal those of hydrochlorothiazide
drugs.adverseEffects: A higher rate of hypokalemia than hydrochlorothiazide, driven by the much longer duration of action

drugs.name: Amiloride
drugs.mechanism: Blocks luminal ENaC in principal cells so the lumen-negative potential is neutralized and ROMK can no longer secrete potassium; it enters the nephron by organic cation transporters rather than OATs
drugs.indication: Potassium-sparing adjunct to a thiazide or loop, lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus where it blocks lithium entry and preserves AQP2, and Liddle syndrome
drugs.adverseEffects: Hyperkalemia, especially with advanced age, renal impairment, hypoaldosteronism, RAS inhibitors, NSAIDs or potassium supplements

drugs.name: Triamterene
drugs.mechanism: Direct ENaC blockade in the cortical collecting duct, abolishing the electrical gradient that drives potassium secretion
drugs.indication: Combined with a thiazide to offset hypokalemia in hypertension and edema
drugs.adverseEffects: Hyperkalemia, triamterene stones, and a risk of interstitial nephritis

drugs.name: Spironolactone
drugs.mechanism: Crosses the basolateral membrane to antagonize the cytosolic mineralocorticoid receptor, blocking transcription of ENaC, Na+/K+ ATPase and ROMK, with an effect proportional to the prevailing aldosterone level
drugs.indication: Primary aldosteronism, HFrEF and HFpEF, cirrhotic ascites, resistant hypertension, and acne or hirsutism through its antiandrogen activity
drugs.adverseEffects: Hyperkalemia plus off-target steroid receptor effects — gynecomastia, impotence, loss of libido, and falsely elevated digoxin assays

drugs.name: Eplerenone
drugs.mechanism: Selective mineralocorticoid receptor antagonism that spares androgen and progesterone receptors, cleared by CYP3A4 to inactive metabolites over a 7-9 hour duration
drugs.indication: Heart failure and hypertension in a patient who cannot tolerate the endocrine effects of spironolactone
drugs.adverseEffects: Hyperkalemia, and interaction with CYP3A4 inhibitors and grapefruit juice, but no gynecomastia

drugs.name: Finerenone
drugs.mechanism: Nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist with a tissue distribution different from the steroidal agents
drugs.indication: Chronic kidney disease, particularly with type 2 diabetes, to slow progression
drugs.adverseEffects: Hyperkalemia, requiring potassium monitoring at initiation

drugs.name: Mannitol
drugs.mechanism: An inert sugar distributed through the ECF that is freely filtered and never reabsorbed, holding water osmotically in the proximal tubule and descending limb
drugs.indication: Raised intracranial pressure with cerebral edema, dropping ICP within 15-30 minutes for 1.5-6 hours, and raised intraocular pressure; IV bolus only
drugs.adverseEffects: Pulmonary edema from the preload surge, hyponatremia in renal impairment, then dehydration with hypernatremia and hyperkalemia

transporters.name: NCC (Na+-Cl- cotransporter)
transporters.location: Apical membrane of the distal convoluted tubule
transporters.function: Reabsorbs 5-10% of the filtered sodium load in a water-impermeable segment, so it dilutes tubular fluid without touching the medullary gradient and concentrating ability stays intact
transporters.regulation: Upregulated during chronic loop diuretic use as part of the distal nephron remodeling that produces diuretic resistance

transporters.name: TRPV5
transporters.location: Apical membrane of the distal convoluted tubule
transporters.function: The entry step for regulated calcium reabsorption, which is why thiazides lower urinary calcium and reduce stone recurrence
transporters.regulation: Driven by the basolateral Na+/Ca2+ exchanger NCX1 (3 Na+ in, 1 Ca2+ out) and fine-tuned by PMCA1b
transporters.inhibitor: Not directly blocked — thiazides raise its activity by lowering intracellular sodium

transporters.name: TRPM6
transporters.location: Apical membrane of the distal convoluted tubule
transporters.function: The regulated magnesium entry pathway of the DCT
transporters.regulation: Downregulated by the DCT remodeling that follows chronic thiazide exposure
transporters.inhibitor: Chronic thiazide therapy indirectly, producing hypomagnesemia

transporters.name: URAT1
transporters.location: Apical membrane of the proximal tubule
transporters.function: Reabsorbs filtered urate back into the blood, setting the serum uric acid level
transporters.regulation: Reabsorption rises with hypovolemia, which is why any volume-depleting diuretic raises urate and can trigger gout
transporters.inhibitor: Probenecid, which blocks reabsorption and is uricosuric

transporters.name: 11-beta-HSD Type 2
transporters.location: Cytosol of the principal cell, alongside the mineralocorticoid receptor
transporters.function: Converts cortisol to inactive cortisone so that cortisol, which binds the mineralocorticoid receptor as well as aldosterone does, cannot activate it
transporters.regulation: Overwhelmed by very high cortisol, or blocked pharmacologically, producing apparent mineralocorticoid excess

transporters.name: SGLT2
transporters.location: Apical membrane of the early proximal tubule
transporters.function: Reabsorbs filtered glucose; blocking it spills glucose into the urine and the extra solute makes the drug behave as a mild osmotic diuretic
transporters.regulation: Load-dependent, saturating above the transport maximum
